problem.title: Preventing Kafka Consumer Rebalance Storms
problem.prompt: A 24-pod Java payment-ledger consumer group reading 48 partitions at 18,000 msg/s enters a continuous rebalance loop whenever the downstream PostgreSQL ledger experiences a 90s lock spike. Each poll() fetches 500 records, pushing batch processing past max.poll.interval.ms=300000, causing LeaveGroup/rebalance storms and zero net commit progress.

spark.summary: A slow downstream dependency stalls batch processing beyond 300s, triggering GroupCoordinator eviction, stop-the-world rebalances, and duplicate redelivery across all 48 partitions.
spark.keyTakeaway: Decouple poll() liveness from slow processing via small max.poll.records, bounded worker queues with pause()/resume(), and CooperativeStickyAssignor.
spark.byteSummary:
**Core Mechanics:** A 24-pod Java payment-ledger consumer group reading **48 partitions at 18,000 msg/s** (1 GiB heap, 2 vCPU) enters a continuous rebalance loop whenever Postgres p99 write latency spikes from **12 ms to 450 ms**.

**Visual & Structural Flow:** Depicts max.poll.interval.ms Eviction vs. pause()/resume() Backpressure (Kafka Broker (48p) -> Poll Thread -> Bounded Queue -> Postgres (450ms)); Active Polling vs. Paused Heartbeat Preservation (ACTIVE POLL -> PAUSED (LIVENESS) -> COMMIT & RESUME).

**Trade-Offs & Production:** Raising `max.poll.interval.ms` to 30 minutes hides genuinely deadlocked consumers for half an hour before recovery. Decouple Kafka group liveness from downstream Postgres latency: **Bound Batch Size**: Lower `max.poll.records` from 500 to `50–100` so worst-case 450 ms DB batches finish well within `max.poll.interval.ms`.

**Failure Modes & Application:** Poll-liveness decoupling is essential in high-throughput Kafka consumers: **Database & External API Sinks**: Protects consumer groups when downstream Postgres, Elasticsearch, or payment APIs experience transient latency spikes.

learningJourney.title: Why Preventing Kafka Consumer Rebalance Storms Matters
learningJourney.explanation: A 24-pod Java payment-ledger consumer group reading **48 partitions at 18,000 msg/s** (1 GiB heap, 2 vCPU) enters a continuous rebalance loop whenever Postgres p99 write latency spikes from **12 ms to 450 ms**. Because each `poll()` fetches **500 records**, batch processing exceeds `max.poll.interval.ms = 300000`, triggering `LeaveGroup` and stop-the-world rebalances that stall all 48 partitions.
learningJourney.purpose: The mechanism: understand how Why Preventing Kafka Consumer Rebalance Storms Matters works from first principles.

learningJourney.title: Real-World Impact of Poll-Interval Rebalance Storms
learningJourney.explanation:
Mixing slow DB I/O with eager `poll()` loops triggers a self-sustaining storm:

1. **Ejected Healthy Consumers**: Exceeding `max.poll.interval.ms` makes the coordinator evict the pod even though its background heartbeat thread is alive.
2. **Duplicate Reprocessing**: Uncommitted batches on the evicted pod are re-delivered to the new owner, piling *more* duplicate work onto the struggling Postgres DB.
3. **Stop-the-World Rebalances**: Default `RangeAssignor` revokes all 48 partitions across all 24 pods on every rebalance.

learningJourney.title: Naive Solution (and Why It Breaks)
learningJourney.explanation: Raising `max.poll.interval.ms` to 30 minutes hides genuinely deadlocked consumers for half an hour before recovery. Spawning unbounded async threads inside `poll()` without `pause()` causes 1 GiB JVM OOMs and commits offsets out of order before DB writes succeed.
learningJourney.purpose: The problem: see what breaks without Naive Solution under real concurrency or scale.

learningJourney.title: Enterprise Solution: `max.poll.records=100`, `pause()/resume()` & `CooperativeStickyAssignor`
learningJourney.explanation:
Decouple Kafka group liveness from downstream Postgres latency:

- **Bound Batch Size**: Lower `max.poll.records` from 500 to `50–100` so worst-case 450 ms DB batches finish well within `max.poll.interval.ms`.
- **Decoupled Worker Queue + `pause()`/`resume()`**: Dispatch polled records to a bounded per-partition worker queue. When the queue fills during a 90s DB lock spike, call `consumer.pause(assignment)` and keep calling `consumer.poll(Duration.ZERO)` so `max.poll.interval.ms` never expires—then `resume()` and commit contiguous offsets once drained.
- **Cooperative Rebalancing + Static Membership**: Set `partition.assignment.strategy=CooperativeStickyAssignor` and `group.instance.id` so rolling deploys move only affected partitions without stopping healthy pods.

sectionDiagram.summary: Pausing partition fetch while keeping poll() spinning prevents rebalance storms without risking OOM.

learningJourney.title: Where Rebalance-Storm Prevention Applies in System Design
learningJourney.explanation:
Poll-liveness decoupling is essential in high-throughput Kafka consumers:

- **Database & External API Sinks**: Protects consumer groups when downstream Postgres, Elasticsearch, or payment APIs experience transient latency spikes.
- **Large Stateful Fleet Upgrades**: `CooperativeStickyAssignor` + `group.instance.id` eliminates stop-the-world pauses during Kubernetes rolling restarts.
- **Bounded-Memory Containers**: Keeps 1 GiB heap pods safe under backpressure.
learningJourney.purpose: Scope boundary: identify where this pattern fits best and where simpler or async alternatives win.

knowledgeCheck.question: Why does calling `consumer.pause(assignment)` while continuing to call `consumer.poll()` prevent a rebalance storm during a 90s Postgres slowdown?

options.text: It stops fetching new records (preventing OOM) while still calling `poll()` to reset the `max.poll.interval.ms` timer and maintain group membership
options.feedback: Correct: `pause()` applies backpressure without letting the coordinator evict the consumer.

options.text: It tells Kafka brokers to delete uncommitted messages from partition 0..47
options.feedback: Messages remain safely in Kafka until the consumer resumes and commits offsets.

options.text: It disables `CooperativeStickyAssignor` during the DB spike
options.feedback: `CooperativeStickyAssignor` remains active and only governs partition assignment.

_nextProblem.title: Preventing Pod OOMKilled (Exit Code 137) Outages
_nextProblem.prompt: A high-throughput Java 21 gRPC/Netty microservice running in Kubernetes is configured with -Xmx4g and container resources.limits.memory=4608Mi. Under peak traffic (12,000 RPS with 64 KB payloads), pods suddenly crash with Exit Code 137 (OOMKilled) even though Prometheus JVM heap metrics show heap usage at only 2.8 GiB (70%) and zero OutOfMemoryError exceptions in application logs. Design a memory-budgeting, off-heap bounding, and observability strategy to eliminate silent cgroup OOM kills.

_problemQuestions.prompt: A user edits their bio and refreshes the page, only to see the old bio for 2 seconds because the read hit a lagging replica. Which consistency guarantee was violated?

options.explanation: Read-Your-Writes ensures a client always observes its own completed writes.
The write was durable on the primary; the replica simply lagged.
Atomicity governs all-or-nothing commit, not cross-replica visibility.

_problemQuestions.prompt: Why does placing `request_timestamp` at the very beginning of a 3,000-token system prompt hurt latency and cost?

options.explanation: BPE still tokenizes the text normally.

options.text: It invalidates prefix/KV caching for all subsequent 3,000 tokens on every request
options.explanation: Correct! Prefix KV caching requires an exact token match from index 0 onward.
Output length is unaffected; Prefill cache reuse is what breaks.
